extraction.name: SciQ
extraction.description: SciQ is a dataset of 13,679 multiple choice science exam questions crowdsourced using a novel method that leverages domain-specific textbooks and model-generated answer distractor suggestions. Each question includes a question, four answer options, and an associated passage used to generate the question. The dataset supports both a multiple choice setting and a direct-answer reading comprehension setting.
extraction.creator: Johannes Welbl (University College London); Nelson F. Liu (University of Washington); Matt Gardner (Allen Institute for Artificial Intelligence)
extraction.citeAs: Johannes Welbl, Nelson F. Liu, and Matt Gardner. 2017. Crowdsourcing Multiple Choice Science Questions. arXiv:1707.06209v1 [cs.HC].
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Questions were crowdsourced via Amazon Mechanical Turk using a two-step process: first, workers were shown filtered passages from science textbooks and asked to formulate a question and correct answer; second, a different set of workers validated the question and selected or wrote answer distractors, aided by model-generated distractor suggestions. A total of 175 workers participated, with AMT Master's status required.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Web Scraping; Manual Human Curator; User-generated content data
extraction.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: In 12.1% of cases, workers rejected all three presented document options and did not generate a question. Additionally, a small percentage of passages were obtained from unreleasable texts, resulting in the direct answer version of SciQ being smaller than the multiple choice version.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Science study textbooks from CK-12 and OpenStax (28 books covering biology, chemistry, earth science, and physics, from elementary to college introductory level), shared under Creative Commons licenses. A set of 3,705 existing 4th and 8th grade science exam questions was used to train the distractor ranking model.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Two-step crowdsourcing process: (1) Workers were shown three filtered textbook paragraphs, chose one, and wrote a question answerable from that passage; instructions specified no yes/no questions, question length 6-30 words, answer length up to 3 words, no ambiguous questions, querying general principles. (2) A second worker validated the (question, answer) pair (marking it as ungrammatical, false answer, unrelated to science, or requiring very specific knowledge) and selected up to two model-suggested distractors plus wrote at least one distractor themselves. AMT Master's status was required for both tasks. 175 workers participated in total.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Questions failing quality control in the distractor selection task (marked as ungrammatical, having a false answer, unrelated to science, or requiring very specific background knowledge) were excluded; 92.8% of questions passed. A qualitative evaluation task asked people to distinguish crowdsourced questions from original exam questions; the original was identified in 55% of cases, below the p=0.05 significance threshold.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: Random forest distractor ranking model trained on 3705 science exam questions (using GloVe embeddings, WordNet, OpenIE-based KB from Simple Wikipedia, POS features, and other features) to suggest top-6 answer distractors; rule-based document filter to classify sentences/paragraphs as relevant or irrelevant
extraction.rai:dataBiases: Questions are derived from a limited set of 28 science study textbooks (biology, chemistry, earth science, physics) spanning elementary to college introductory level, which constrains the topical and linguistic diversity of the dataset; crowd workers without domain expertise may produce questions lacking relevance or diversity in structure and content
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: A small percentage of the passages were obtained from unreleasable texts, so the direct answer version of SciQ is slightly smaller; neural models do not beat simple information retrieval baselines on the multiple choice version, suggesting limitations for neural model applicability; the distractor model quality is not high enough to use predictions directly without additional filtering by crowd workers
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Training and evaluation of science exam question answering systems; investigating neural model performance in medium-sized data settings; augmenting training data for answering real 4th and 8th grade science exam questions; reading comprehension research in both multiple choice and direct answer settings
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: The dataset construction involved model-assisted augmentation of answer distractors: a random forest classifier trained on real science exam questions ranked candidate distractors from a pool of 488,819 expressions, and the top six suggestions were presented to crowd workers. Workers could select up to two model-generated distractors and were required to write at least one themselves, resulting in 36.1% of final distractors being model-generated. Additionally, SciQ was used as supplementary training data to augment existing 4th and 8th grade science exam question datasets for downstream model training.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: A rule-based document filter was applied to individual paragraphs of the base corpus to select suitable passages for question generation. Sentences were filtered out if they: were a question or exclamation, had no verb phrase, contained modal verbs, contained imperative phrases, contained demonstrative pronouns, contained personal pronouns other than third-person, began with a pronoun, contained first names, had less than 6 or more than 18 tokens or more than 2 commas, contained special characters other than punctuation, had more than three tokens beginning uppercase, mentioned a graph, table or web link, began with a discourse marker, contained absolute wording, or contained instructional vocabulary. A paragraph was accepted only if a minimum number of its sentences passed these filters. Additionally, questions failing quality control in the distractor selection task (marked as ungrammatical, having a false answer, being unrelated to science, or requiring very specific background knowledge) were excluded; 92.8% of questions passed this check.
